content: Hypertension, also known as high blood pressure (HTN), is a chronic medical condition characterized by persistently elevated blood pressure levels. The term hypertension typically refers to arterial hypertension unless otherwise specified. Blood pressure is the force exerted by circulating blood against the walls of the arteries. It is highest during the heart's contraction phase, known as systolic pressure, and lowest during the relaxation phase between beats, referred to as diastolic pressure. Hypertension is diagnosed when systolic blood pressure consistently measures 140 mmHg or higher, and/or diastolic blood pressure is 90 mmHg or higher. According to the Seventh Report of the Joint National Committee (JNC 7) in 2003, blood pressure readings between 120/80 mmHg and 139/89 mmHg are classified as prehypertension. This category is not a disease but rather a warning sign for individuals at increased risk of developing hypertension. The Mayo Clinic suggests that a blood pressure below 120/80 mmHg is normal, with some evidence indicating that 115/75 mmHg may be an ideal target. For patients with diabetes or kidney disease, blood pressure above 130/80 mmHg is considered high and warrants treatment. Home blood pressure monitoring devices may detect hypertension at even lower thresholds. Symptoms of Hypertension Hypertension is often asymptomatic, meaning most individuals do not experience noticeable symptoms. It is frequently discovered during routine medical visits or blood pressure checks. However, untreated hypertension can silently cause damage to the heart, kidneys, and other organs. In rare cases, severe hypertension may present with symptoms such as intense headaches, nausea, vomiting, confusion, visual disturbances, or nosebleeds. These symptoms may indicate a hypertensive emergency, requiring immediate medical attention. Causes of Hypertension Hypertension can be classified into two main types: essential (primary) hypertension and secondary hypertension. Essential Hypertension The exact cause of essential hypertension is unknown, but several factors contribute to its development: Sedentary lifestyle Obesity, which accounts for 80-85% of cases High salt intake Excessive alcohol consumption Vitamin D deficiency Family history of hypertension Genetic predispositions Overactivation of the renin-angiotensin system, which regulates blood pressure High fructose corn syrup consumption Metabolic syndrome, characterized by insulin resistance, obesity, high blood pressure, and abnormal cholesterol levels Secondary Hypertension Secondary hypertension results from identifiable underlying causes and requires targeted treatment. Common causes include: Renovascular Hypertension: Narrowing of the renal arteries due to fibromuscular dysplasia or renal artery stenosis. Pheochromocytoma: Excessive secretion of norepinephrine and epinephrine, leading to vasoconstriction. Hyperaldosteronism (Conn's Syndrome): Overproduction of aldosterone, often due to adrenal gland disorders. Cushing's Syndrome: Excessive glucocorticoid secretion. Hyperparathyroidism Acromegaly Thyroid Disorders: Both hyperthyroidism and hypothyroidism. Chronic Kidney Disease Coarctation of the Aorta Medications: Certain drugs, such as oral contraceptives, steroids, NSAIDs, nasal decongestants, and MAO inhibitors, can elevate blood pressure. Obstructive Sleep Apnea White Coat Hypertension: Elevated blood pressure in clinical settings due to anxiety. Perioperative Hypertension: Blood pressure elevation around the time of surgery due to factors like pain, hypothermia, or fluid overload. Risk Factors Individuals at higher risk for hypertension include those with: High salt intake Obesity Smoking habits Excessive alcohol consumption Family history of hypertension Diets high in cholesterol Certain personality traits, such as impatience, high anxiety, or hostility Low socioeconomic status or chronic stress Diagnosis Hypertension is diagnosed after multiple blood pressure readings taken at different times. Blood pressure naturally fluctuates throughout the day, so home monitoring may provide a more accurate assessment than readings taken in a clinical setting. It is essential to use a high-quality home device with a properly sized cuff and digital readout. Patients should practice taking their blood pressure under the guidance of a healthcare provider to ensure accuracy. A physical examination may also be performed to detect signs of heart disease, eye damage, or other complications. When to Seek Urgent Medical Care Patients should have their blood pressure checked every two years if it is below 120/80 mmHg and annually if it falls within the prehypertension range (120-139/80-89 mmHg). Urgent medical care is necessary if blood pressure exceeds 120/80 mmHg and is accompanied by severe headaches, visual disturbances, dizziness, chest pain, limb weakness, nausea, vomiting, or fatigue. Hypertension can lead to complications affecting the heart, brain, eyes, kidneys, and nervous system. Management and Lifestyle Modifications Hypertension can often be managed through lifestyle changes, including: Reducing dietary sodium to less than 1,500 mg per day Avoiding high-fat and fried foods Following a DASH (Dietary Approaches to Stop Hypertension) diet rich in fruits and vegetables Exercising regularly as recommended by a healthcare provider Avoiding high-cholesterol foods Increasing dietary fiber intake Limiting alcohol consumption Medications Several classes of medications are used to treat hypertension: Diuretics: Reduce salt and water retention. Beta Blockers: Lower heart rate and blood pressure. ACE Inhibitors: Decrease angiotensin levels, reducing blood pressure. Calcium Channel Blockers: Prevent calcium from entering arterial walls, reducing arterial narrowing. Angiotensin II Receptor Blockers (ARBs): Directly lower angiotensin levels. Alpha Blockers: Reduce arterial narrowing. Combined Alpha/Beta Blockers: Act on both alpha and beta receptors to lower blood pressure. Centrally Acting Antihypertensives: Act on the brain to reduce blood pressure. Direct Vasodilators: Prevent arterial narrowing, often used in special conditions like pregnancy. Medications to Avoid Patients with chronic or uncontrolled hypertension should avoid certain medications, including: Antiplatelet agents like abciximab Thrombolytics like alteplase and reteplase Erythropoiesis-stimulating agents like epoetin alfa Appetite suppressants like phentermine Nasal decongestants like phenylephrine Triptans for migraines, such as rizatriptan and zolmitriptan Always consult a physician before starting or discontinuing any medication. Prognosis and Complications Hypertension is a manageable condition, but it requires lifelong attention to diet, exercise, and medication adherence. If left untreated, it can lead to severe complications, including heart disease, stroke, kidney failure, vision loss, and nerve damage. Maintaining a healthy lifestyle is crucial for preventing these outcomes.
